plain_text:
At some point during the composition
of "Rhapsody in Blue," one of George
Gershwin's masterpieces of 20th-century
music, he got help with the process: After
all, the piece, which was to debut in just
a few short weeks, eventually would run
to 22,000 notes over 500 measures.

made as the piece came together.

plain_text:
The vast collections of the division
document the birth of “Rhapsody.” It holds
four manuscripts of the piece, including
Gershwin’s original manuscript, now
digitized. That manuscript is in pencil,
with “RHAPSODY IN BLUE – FOR JAZZ
BAND AND PIANO” written across the top
of the first page in neat block lettering.
It is dated Jan. 7, 1924, a few days after
Gershwin agreed to compose a piece for an
upcoming concert by Whiteman’s band.

plain_text:
The Library also holds the papers
of Grofé, who provided the score
for the 1942 orchestral version that
quickly became the standard.
semantic_text: The Library also holds the papers of Grofé, who provided the score for the 1942 orchestral version that quickly became the standard.

plain_text:
Taken together, the two collections give the
Library all the manuscripts of “Rhapsody”
leading up to its historic debut just over a
century ago, on Feb. 12, 1924, at Aeolian
Hall – its long, opening glissando on clarinet
signaling a new era in American music.
